subChunks.title: Astronomy & Cosmology

storyBeats.txt: Every atom of carbon in your body was forged in the core of a star that died before the Sun was born, Theodora said. The iron in your blood was created in a supernova. You are, in the most literal sense, made of stardust. Astronomy is not a subject remote from everyday life. It is the history of the atoms you are made of.

The universe began 13.8 billion years ago in an event we call the Big Bang. Not an explosion in space — but an explosion of space itself. In the first three minutes, the lightest elements were forged. In the first billion years, galaxies formed. In the last few billion years, the Sun, the Earth, and eventually you.

And yet for all of that — for all of the 13.8 billion years and the 2 trillion galaxies we can observe — we still do not know what 95% of the universe is made of. Dark matter and dark energy are the names we give to our ignorance. That, too, is science.

subChunks.hookHtml: Astronomy is the oldest science — humans have studied the night sky for as long as they have kept records. Modern astronomy has extended our vision across 13.8 billion years of cosmic history, from the Big Bang to the formation of the solar system to the atmospheres of distant exoplanets. Understanding the universe's structure, scale, and history is both a profound intellectual achievement and the context within which all Earth science sits.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Scale of the Universe

The universe is almost incomprehensibly large. Useful distance units:

  • Astronomical Unit (AU): Average Earth-Sun distance = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m (~150 million km). Used within the solar system.
  • Light-year (ly): Distance light travels in one year = 9.461 × 10¹⁵ m. Proxima Centauri (nearest star): 4.24 ly. Milky Way diameter: ~100,000 ly.
  • Parsec (pc): 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m = 3.26 ly. Used by professional astronomers. Megaparsec (Mpc) for intergalactic distances.

The observable universe extends ~46 billion light-years in all directions (despite being only 13.8 billion years old — space itself has been expanding). The Milky Way contains roughly 200–400 billion stars. The observable universe contains an estimated 2 trillion galaxies.

The Solar System

The Sun contains 99.86% of the solar system's mass. Structure: core (nuclear fusion, 15 million °C), radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere (visible surface, ~5,500°C), chromosphere, corona (~1–3 million °C — why the corona is hotter than the surface is an unsolved problem).

Planets: eight planets in order from the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (terrestrial — rocky, dense, small), Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (gas/ice giants — massive, low density, thick atmospheres). The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter; the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune; the Oort Cloud (hypothetical, source of long-period comets) extends to ~50,000 AU.

Planet formation: the solar nebula hypothesis — the solar system formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust ~4.6 billion years ago. Conservation of angular momentum caused the collapsing cloud to spin and flatten into an accretion disc; the Sun formed at the centre while planets accreted from dust and planetesimals in the disc.

The Life Cycle of Stars

Stars are powered by nuclear fusion in their cores. The main sequence (H-R diagram) is where most stars spend most of their lives, fusing hydrogen to helium. Star mass determines lifespan: massive stars burn hotter and faster (millions of years); low-mass stars burn slowly (trillions of years for red dwarfs).

Stellar evolution:

  • Sun-like stars: Main sequence (~10 billion years) → red giant (core collapses; outer layers expand) → planetary nebula (outer layers expelled) → white dwarf (dense, hot, cooling remnant; Earth-sized but Sun-mass).
  • Massive stars (>8 solar masses): Main sequence (millions of years) → red supergiant → supernova explosion → neutron star or (if >25 solar masses) black hole. Supernovae synthesise and disperse heavy elements (iron and heavier) — stellar nucleosynthesis is the origin of all elements heavier than iron.

The H-R (Hertzsprung-Russell) diagram plots stellar luminosity vs temperature. The main sequence runs from hot/bright (top left) to cool/dim (bottom right). Giants occupy upper right; white dwarfs occupy lower left.

Galaxies

A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter. Types:

  • Spiral: Disc shape with spiral arms — younger stars and star formation in arms; older stars in bulge and halo. The Milky Way and Andromeda are spirals.
  • Elliptical: Roughly spherical or ellipsoidal; mostly old red stars; little ongoing star formation.
  • Irregular: No defined structure; often disturbed by gravitational interaction with neighbours. Magellanic Clouds are irregular galaxies.

The Milky Way is part of the Local Group (30+ galaxies). The Local Group is part of the Virgo Supercluster. The universe is structured as a cosmic web — filaments and sheets of galaxy clusters surrounding vast voids.

The Big Bang and Cosmology

Evidence for the Big Bang:

  • Hubble's Law (1929): Galaxies are receding from us at speeds proportional to their distance (v = H₀d). The universe is expanding — run the expansion backward and everything was once at a single point.
  • Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB): Uniform microwave radiation filling the universe in all directions — the afterglow of the hot early universe, from 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form (recombination) and photons to travel freely. Discovered by Penzias and Wilson (1964, Nobel Prize 1978).
  • Big Bang nucleosynthesis: Predicted abundances of hydrogen (~75%), helium (~25%), and trace lithium from fusion in the first 3 minutes — match observed cosmic abundances.

Key timeline: Big Bang (t=0) → quark-gluon plasma (10⁻⁶ s) → protons/neutrons form → nucleosynthesis (first 3 min) → recombination and CMB emission (380,000 yr) → first stars (200 million yr) → galaxy formation (1 billion yr) → solar system forms (9.2 billion yr after BB) → now (13.8 billion yr).

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

Dark matter (~27% of universe's energy): Matter that does not interact electromagnetically (cannot emit, absorb, or reflect light) but exerts gravitational effects. Evidence: galaxy rotation curves (stars at galaxy edges rotate too fast to be held by visible mass alone); gravitational lensing; galaxy cluster dynamics. Composition unknown — leading candidates include WIMPs and axions.

Dark energy (~68% of universe's energy): A mysterious energy density causing the universe's expansion to accelerate (discovered 1998, Nobel Prize 2011). May be Einstein's cosmological constant (Λ) — vacuum energy of empty space. Nature completely unknown.

Ordinary matter (everything we can see and detect) constitutes only ~5% of the universe's total energy budget.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how we know the universe started with a Big Bang — what evidence could scientists possibly have for something that happened 13.8 billion years ago?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: The star Betelgeuse (in Orion) is a red supergiant approximately 700 times the radius of the Sun, with a mass of roughly 15–20 solar masses. (1) Using your knowledge of stellar evolution, predict what will happen to Betelgeuse at the end of its life. (2) Betelgeuse is approximately 700 light-years from Earth. When astronomers observe it today, how old is the light they are seeing? (3) Astronomers observed Betelgeuse dimming significantly in 2019-2020. One hypothesis was that it was about to go supernova. If it were to go supernova, would it be visible from Earth in daylight? (4) Supernovae are described as 'cosmic element factories.' Explain what this means in terms of nucleosynthesis.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Betelgeuse, with 15–20 solar masses, is a massive star. Its evolution: it is already in the red supergiant phase (post-main-sequence). It will undergo a core collapse supernova — the core will implode when silicon fusion can no longer support it against gravity (iron fusion is endothermic and does not release energy). The outer layers will be violently expelled in the supernova explosion. The remnant will be a neutron star (if core mass < ~3 solar masses) or possibly a black hole. The supernova will also produce a neutron star/pulsar and a supernova remnant nebula (like the Crab Nebula).

(2) Light travels at approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The light astronomers observe from Betelgeuse today left the star approximately 700 years ago — around the 14th century CE. We are not seeing Betelgeuse as it is now; we see it as it was ~700 years ago. If Betelgeuse had already gone supernova 500 years ago, we would not know yet. We are always observing the past when we look at distant objects.

(3) Yes — Betelgeuse at supernova would be extraordinarily bright. Type II supernovae can reach absolute magnitude around −17 to −18. Betelgeuse at ~700 light-years would appear comparable in brightness to the full Moon or brighter — easily visible in daylight for weeks. Historical supernovae that were visible in daylight include SN 1054 (the Crab Nebula progenitor, visible for 23 days in daylight) at ~6,500 light-years. Betelgeuse is much closer; it would be spectacular. The 2019–2020 dimming was subsequently explained by a dust cloud from surface mass ejection — not imminent supernova.

(4) Stellar nucleosynthesis — supernovae as 'cosmic element factories': Stars on the main sequence fuse hydrogen to helium (H→He). In later stages, stars fuse helium to carbon, carbon to neon, silicon, and eventually iron in successive burning shells. Elements up to iron (Fe, atomic number 26) are produced by successive fusion stages (exothermic up to iron). Iron fusion is endothermic — no more energy release, triggering core collapse. During the supernova explosion itself, the intense flux of neutrons drives rapid neutron capture (r-process), synthesising elements heavier than iron — gold, uranium, silver, and most other heavy elements. These elements are then scattered into interstellar space by the explosion, eventually becoming incorporated into new solar nebulae — and into planets, and into us. All elements heavier than iron in our bodies (and most from carbon to iron) were made in stars.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Explain Hubble's Law and why it is evidence for the Big Bang. Your answer should include: (1) what Hubble observed in 1929; (2) the mathematical relationship between recession speed and distance; (3) what the Hubble constant tells us about the age of the universe; (4) why the expansion of the universe does not mean we are at the centre; and (5) what additional evidence from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) supports the Big Bang model.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) In 1929, Edwin Hubble observed that distant galaxies show redshifted spectra — their spectral lines are shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths compared to laboratory standards. This redshift is a Doppler effect: the galaxies are moving away from us. Crucially, Hubble found that the more distant a galaxy is, the faster it is receding. This was the first direct evidence that the universe is not static but expanding.

(2) Hubble's Law: v = H₀ × d, where v is the recession velocity of a galaxy, d is its distance, and H₀ is the Hubble constant (currently measured at ~67–73 km/s/Mpc — there is a 'Hubble tension' between different measurement methods). The relationship is linear: double the distance, double the recession speed. This is what you would expect if space itself is expanding uniformly — every point in the universe is moving away from every other point.

(3) The Hubble constant gives the current expansion rate. Extrapolating the expansion backward (making simplifying assumptions about expansion history), 1/H₀ gives an estimate of the universe's age. Current best estimates give an age of approximately 13.8 billion years. More precisely, the age depends on the full cosmological model (including dark energy and dark matter), giving 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years from CMB data.

(4) The expansion does not mean we are at the centre for the same reason that the surface of an expanding balloon has no centre. If you draw dots on a balloon and inflate it, every dot moves away from every other dot — no single dot is the 'centre' of the expansion. The expansion is in the fabric of space itself, not an explosion from a single point in existing space. An observer in any galaxy would see all other galaxies receding from them — everyone appears to be at the centre. There is no preferred location.

(5) CMB evidence: The Cosmic Microwave Background is uniform microwave radiation (blackbody spectrum at 2.725 K, peaking in microwaves) that fills the universe in all directions, discovered accidentally by Penzias and Wilson in 1964. It is the afterglow of the hot early universe. When the universe was ~380,000 years old, it cooled enough (~3,000 K) for protons and electrons to combine into neutral hydrogen atoms (recombination). Before this, the universe was opaque — photons scattered off free electrons. After recombination, photons could travel freely; these are the CMB photons we detect today, redshifted by 1,100× to microwave wavelengths by cosmic expansion. The CMB: (a) has exactly the spectrum predicted by a hot Big Bang origin; (b) is isotropic to 1 part in 100,000 — consistent with a hot, uniform early universe; (c) shows tiny temperature fluctuations (anisotropies) that match predictions for quantum fluctuations in the early universe, which became the seeds of today's galaxy structure — confirmed in detail by COBE, WMAP, and Planck satellite missions. No other cosmological model predicts all of these properties.
learningObjectives: Describe the scale of the solar system, the Milky Way, and the observable universe using appropriate distance units (AU, light-year, parsec).
Outline the life cycle of Sun-like and massive stars, identifying the end states (white dwarf, neutron star, black hole) and explaining why stellar mass determines the outcome.
State the three main pieces of evidence for the Big Bang (Hubble's Law, CMB, nucleosynthesis abundances) and explain what each demonstrates.
Explain what dark matter and dark energy are, what evidence supports their existence, and why they are called 'dark'.
commonMistakes: Thinking the Big Bang was an explosion in space — it was an expansion of space itself; there was no pre-existing empty space into which matter exploded.
Assuming we are at the centre of the expanding universe — Hubble's Law applies equally from every vantage point; no location is privileged.
Confusing light-year with a unit of time — a light-year is a unit of distance (the distance light travels in one year), not a duration.
Thinking massive stars live longer than low-mass stars — massive stars burn their fuel far faster despite having more of it; they live millions of years, while red dwarfs may live trillions.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly describes the end states of Sun-like and massive stars and explains the role of mass in determining the outcome.
Explains Hubble's Law mathematically (v = H₀d) and uses it to explain both cosmic expansion and the estimated age of the universe.
Describes the Cosmic Microwave Background — what it is physically, when it was emitted, and why it is evidence for the Big Bang.
Explains why dark matter is inferred from gravitational effects rather than direct observation, with at least one specific line of evidence.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The thermal radiation filling the universe — the afterglow of the hot early universe from 380,000 years after the Big Bang; temperature 2.725 K; discovered 1964 (Penzias and Wilson); mapped in detail by COBE, WMAP, and Planck satellites.

Hertzsprung-Russell diagram — plots stellar luminosity vs surface temperature (or spectral class); reveals stellar evolution tracks; the main sequence is a diagonal band where most stars spend their hydrogen-burning lives.

The production of elements in stellar interiors and supernovae — elements up to iron are produced by fusion in stars; elements heavier than iron are produced by neutron capture in supernovae (r-process) and neutron star mergers.

A current discrepancy between the Hubble constant measured from CMB data (~67 km/s/Mpc) and from local distance ladder measurements (~73 km/s/Mpc) — significant enough to suggest either systematic errors or new physics beyond the standard cosmological model.

A planet orbiting a star other than the Sun — first confirmed in 1992 (around a pulsar) and 1995 (around a main-sequence star). Over 5,500 confirmed as of 2024, detected primarily by transit photometry (Kepler, TESS) and radial velocity methods.

questions.questionHtml: What is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and why is it evidence for the Big Bang?
options: Microwave radiation emitted by distant microwave sources; evidence that the universe contains many microwave-emitting objects

Thermal radiation filling the universe in all directions — the afterglow of the hot early universe from 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form and photons to travel freely
Background noise from Earth's own microwave emissions, accidentally discovered by Penzias and Wilson
Radiation emitted by the Big Bang itself, still travelling outward from its original location
questions.correctAnswer: Thermal radiation filling the universe in all directions — the afterglow of the hot early universe from 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form and photons to travel freely
questions.explanationHtml: The CMB is thermal blackbody radiation (2.725 K) filling the universe isotropically. Before recombination (380,000 years after the Big Bang), the universe was opaque — photons scattered continuously off free electrons in the plasma. When the universe cooled to ~3,000 K, protons and electrons combined into neutral hydrogen; photons could then travel freely. Those photons, redshifted by cosmic expansion from ~3,000 K to 2.725 K over 13.8 billion years, are the CMB. Its spectrum, isotropy, and predicted temperature match the Big Bang model with extraordinary precision.

questions.questionHtml: A star has 20 times the mass of our Sun and is currently on the main sequence. Compared to the Sun, what can you predict about this star's lifespan and eventual fate?
options: It will live 20 times longer than the Sun and end as a white dwarf
It will live a fraction of the Sun's lifespan (millions rather than billions of years) and end as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole
It will live the same length of time as the Sun but will end as a neutron star
It will live longer than the Sun because it has more fuel, and will end as a black dwarf
questions.correctAnswer: It will live a fraction of the Sun's lifespan (millions rather than billions of years) and end as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole
questions.explanationHtml: Stellar lifespan scales inversely with mass (approximately as M^{-2.5}): a star 20× more massive than the Sun has roughly 20^{2.5} ≈ 1,800× higher luminosity and burns its fuel proportionally faster. Despite having 20× more hydrogen, it burns ~1,800× faster, giving a main-sequence lifetime ~90× shorter. The Sun will live ~10 billion years; a 20-solar-mass star lives ~10 million years. Its end state: supernova (core collapse when iron builds up in the core), leaving a neutron star or black hole. Only stars with initial mass below ~8 solar masses become white dwarfs.

questions.questionHtml: Astronomers observe that galaxy clusters contain far more mass than can be accounted for by the visible stars and gas. This excess mass is called dark matter. Why can't this simply be explained by the presence of very faint stars, gas, or dust that we haven't detected yet?
options: Because we have directly observed dark matter particles using particle detectors

Because multiple independent lines of evidence (rotation curves, gravitational lensing, CMB anisotropies, large-scale structure) all point to the same total amount of non-luminous matter, and the amount required far exceeds any plausible quantity of ordinary matter that could have escaped detection
Because faint stars and gas do not exist in galaxy clusters
Because dark matter was created at the Big Bang before any stars or gas formed, so stars cannot explain it
questions.correctAnswer: Because multiple independent lines of evidence (rotation curves, gravitational lensing, CMB anisotropies, large-scale structure) all point to the same total amount of non-luminous matter, and the amount required far exceeds any plausible quantity of ordinary matter that could have escaped detection
questions.explanationHtml: The evidence for dark matter is convergent across multiple independent methods. Galaxy rotation curves require ~5–6× more mass than visible matter; gravitational lensing (light bending around clusters) maps mass distributions that don't match visible matter; CMB anisotropies constrain the total matter density to ~32% of the universe's energy content, of which only ~5% can be ordinary (baryonic) matter; large-scale structure simulations only reproduce observed filaments and voids if ~27% dark matter is included. The Bullet Cluster provides direct evidence — two galaxy clusters that have passed through each other show hot gas (X-ray emission) offset from the mass concentration (gravitational lensing) — exactly what you'd expect if most mass is dark matter that passed through while gas was slowed by electromagnetic interactions.
